new_statements.quote: All descriptions of Yuman languages agree that these are stress languages, and that stress is assigned morphologically to the root of the word. The canonical shape of a Yuman root may be reconstructed as a monosyllabic morpheme bearing stress (Langdon 1975) [...] Uninflected words tend to have stress on the last syllable in direct consequence of the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes. [...] Nevertheless, suffixes producing unstressed syllables are common, though they are mostly syntactic in function. [p. 239] Note that regardless of the complexity of the word, the stress remains fixed on the root. [p. 240] Stress is basically morphological, it is a property of the root [p. 252]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's StressTyp2 fixed: final syllable record (final stress): Langdon says uninflected Yuman words tend to have last-syllable stress, and Hyman's own survey in the same volume (p. 64, 'Languages with dominant final stress') lists Yuma from Halpern 1946. But the deciding statement is that stress is morphological, fixed on the root, and that suffixes producing unstressed post-stress syllables are common, so 'final' is the usual surface outcome of root stress rather than a positional rule; adds secondary stress in compounds and the Halpern two-primary-stress cases. The paper gives no Yuma-specific examples; its claim about Yuma is by inclusion in the family-wide general…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement covering Yuma (Quechan), which Langdon places in the River group with Mojave and Maricopa: primary stress sits on the monosyllabic root morpheme wherever it falls in the word. Because Yuman words are built mostly with prefixes and only consonantal derivational suffixes, the root is usually the last syllable, so uninflected words tend to surface with final stress; syntactic suffixes can add unstressed post-stress syllables without moving the stress. Only Mojave (not Yuma) is said to show stress shifts, and those are derived from root stress by retraction rules.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 240: "The only thing that can happen to a stressed syllable is that the stress reduces in compound formation to secondary stress on the first member of the compound, thus maintaining the preference for primary stress on the last syllable. Secondary stress in compounds may also further reduce so as to become indistinguishable from other unstressed material." (examples are Diegueño compounds)
new_statements.exceptions: fn. 4, p. 257: "Some investigators (e.g. Redden 1966 and Halpern 1946-47) describe suffixes which have primary stress so that some 'words' in Yuman have two primary stresses. I have ignored these in this paper on the assumption that these forms function as two words." (Halpern 1946-47 is the Yuma grammar.) p. 240: Mojave is "unique among Yuman languages" in showing stress shifts; pp. 248-249 derive these from underlying root stress plus vowel-length-driven retraction, which Langdon does not extend to Yuma. Post-stress unstressed syllables from syntactic suffixes (p. 239) mean surface stress is not strictly final.
new_statements.identity_note: Langdon 1977 is a family-wide paper; it names Yuma (= Quechan, glottocode quec1382) as a River-group language with Mojave and Maricopa (p. 239) but draws its examples from Diegueño, Cocopa, Kiliwa, Walapai, Paipai, Yavapai and Mojave, none from Yuma. Its statement about Yuma is the generalization "all descriptions of Yuman languages agree", which for Yuma rests on Halpern 1946-47 (IJAL 12-13), the source it cites for Yuma phonology. The Mojave stress-retraction facts (pp. 248-252) concern Mojave only and are said to be unique in the family.

readall_conflicts: No two sources disagree outright. The catalog (StressTyp2) records Quechan as fixed: final syllable; Langdon 1977 states for all Yuman languages, Yuma included, that stress is a morphological property of the root, which surfaces as last-syllable stress in uninflected words because the morphology is prefixing, but syntactic suffixes can add unstressed syllables after the stressed root. Hyman's survey in the same volume lists Yuma under dominant final stress (p. 64) and notes, citing Halpern 1946:150, restricted cases of two phonemic primary stresses in one word (p. 38); Langdon treats those as two-word sequences (fn. 4). The tension is descriptive level (surface final vs underlying root), not placement.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Halpern 1946b IJAL 12(3):150 sec. 16 'Accent') is present verbatim in the held archive.org scanned text at the stated page; Halpern 1946a (Yuma I) and Miller 1997 (held excerpts) independently agree (one accent per stem, on the stem; a few inherently accented suffixes; two-accent words = stem + accented suffix). (2) Deciding source: a first-hand descriptive grammar (Halpern's six-part IJAL Yuma grammar, 1946-47), which Glottolog 5.1 shows is still the only grammar of Quechan and which the modern specialist (Miller 2014, downloaded now) names as the detailed description of Quechan phonology and morphology. No instrumental or later dedicated stress study of Quechan was found. (3) Coding: Halpern's rule is morphologically determined (accent = last vowel of the stem wherever it falls in the word, plus lexically accented suffixes), so no syllable-count/edge r

sources.quote: No stress rule stated. The practical orthography marks the stressed vowel with an acute accent (á, ée ...), distinguishes 'unaccented a' = inorganic (schwa) vowel in pre-stress position and ə in post-stress position, and defers: 'The phonology and morphology of Quechan are described in detail by Halpern (1946, 1947). Further information may be found in Langdon (1977) and Miller (1997).' Text forms throughout show stem accent non-finally and finally (e.g. av'áak, nyaav'áak, kwatsáan), consistent with Halpern's stem-final accent.
